item.title: AI takes spotlight at China-ASEAN Expo
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
People visit the sales area of AI-related products during the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 18, 2026. AI-related products have taken center stage at the ongoing 23rd China-ASEAN Expo, which attracts more than 3,400 companies from China, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and beyond. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming) NANNING, China, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- When Vietnamese visitor Doan Minh Thao stepped into an exhibition hall of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo here on Friday, he got interested in an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered eyewear that can provide real-time translation in over 40 languages, including Vietnamese. With the help of this gadget, developed by a Chinese company, he managed to have unimpeded verbal communication with exhibitors at the venue. AI-related products including these smart glasses have taken center stage at the ongoing Expo, which attracts more than 3,400 companies from China, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and beyond. FROM CONCEPT TO REAL BUSINESS "Last year, AI was mostly for show. This year, it is driving sales," said Wang Jicai, secretary-general of the China-ASEAN Expo Secretariat. In exhibition halls situated in the downtown area of this southern Chinese city, embodied AI robots, exoskeleton medical equipment and AI-enabled wearables attracted crowds of curious visitors, while unattended coffee booths and ice cream stands served customers with nimble robotic arms. As some companies display fancy hardware at the Expo, others showcase AI-driven systems for sectors ranging from finance, healthcare, transportation and agriculture to production management and water treatment. China and ASEAN, trading partners that saw bilateral trade volume top 1 trillion U.S. dollars in 2025, have been organizing this major trade and investment event for more than two decades. And for this year's Expo, which runs from Sept. 17 to 21, special emphasis was placed on the AI sector. According to organizers, the Expo's "AI marketplace" features about 500 products from more than 70 companies, allowing visitors to test and buy products on-site. In the meantime, a China-ASEAN AI application cooperation center has cataloged more than 1,000 potential AI scenarios, set up offices in Vietnam, Laos and Malaysia, and backed over 30 cross-border projects. AI ENABLES BROADER COOPERATION "What inspires me most is seeing that AI is not limited to the technology sector. It can also serve as an enabler for education, healthcare, tourism, industry, public services, agriculture and the development of economic zones," said Dyah Wahyu Ermawati, director of investment and integrated license services office of Indonesia's East Java province. "There are very broad opportunities for cooperation," the Indonesian official said to Xinhua Thursday when attending the 2nd China-ASEAN AI Scenario Application Matchmaking Session organized in Nanning alongside the Expo. China and ASEAN, already each other's biggest trading partner, are seeking to strengthen and upgrade cooperation in a wide range of sectors. The progress in digital technologies including AI has facilitated cooperation and enhanced efficiency. In Laos and Cambodia, for example, a platform developed by local partners together with an enterprise from China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region has started to use satellite imagery, drones and ground sensors to optimize tropical crop cultivation. Apart from precision agriculture, cooperation in AI applications can also include fields like smart logistics, manufacturing automation, financial technology, urban management and cross-border e-commerce, according to exhibitors and seminar speakers at the Expo. AI BRINGS GREAT OPPORTUNITIES As China and ASEAN advance high-quality economic cooperation under the framework of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, signed in October 2025, AI has emerged as a new frontier for win-win cooperation. During a China-ASEAN business and investment summit held here on Thursday, a collection of case studies on China-ASEAN AI cooperation was released, showcasing a range of practical achievements. The cases include 31 practical AI cooperation projects between China and ASEAN, covering all 11 ASEAN member states and sectors such as infrastructure, intelligent manufacturing and smart logistics. "I think there's a lot of optimism that we will be benefiting from this collaboration with AI," Secretary-General of ASEAN Kao Kim Hourn said to reporters Thursday on the sidelines of the Expo. It is not only for the economic sector; it cuts across all sectors of the society, he said. The secretary-general said there are great opportunities to capitalize on the potential of AI and the digital sector. Regarding AI cooperation, he called for adequate rules and regulations and advised against stifling innovation and creativity. ■ A child interacts with a robotic pet at the AI exhibition hall of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 18, 2026. item.title: First-ever orthodontic treatment restores giant panda's normal bite in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
This undated file photo shows the giant panda Beixia at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province. (Xinhua) CHENGDU, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese specialists have successfully corrected a giant panda's crooked jaw using an orthodontic technique adapted from human treatment, in the first such procedure performed on this species. The treatment, jointly carried out by the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding and West China Hospital of Stomatology, restored the panda's ability to bite and chew normally. Related research was published in July in The Angle Orthodontist, a leading international orthodontic journal. Beixia, a male giant panda born in 2022, suffered a jaw injury shortly after birth. By around three months old, his lower jaw had begun to deviate to the left, causing milk to leak from his mouth and raising concerns that he could eventually struggle to chew bamboo, which posed a serious threat to his survival. With Beixia's jaw still developing, veterinarians and orthodontists decided to use the panda's natural growth potential to correct the asymmetry. They digitally scanned his mouth and designed a customized fixed appliance, with three orthodontic elastic bands to apply gentle traction and guide the jaw toward more symmetrical growth. Long Hu, an orthodontist at West China Hospital of Stomatology, said it was the first time a growth-modification technique used in human orthodontics had been applied to a giant panda. "Little was known about jaw development in giant pandas, but for Beixia's health, we decided to take on the challenge," Long said. The treatment lasted about six months. The bands were removed before each feeding and put back afterward. At first, Beixia would push at them with his tongue or paw at his mouth, requiring caregivers to watch closely to prevent the bands from coming loose or being swallowed. Follow-up examinations showed that Beixia's jaw deviation had largely been corrected, and normal sucking, chewing and swallowing functions had been restored. Now four years old, he can eat normally and remains active and playful. The treatment reflects increasingly refined veterinary care for China's captive giant panda population, which reached 808 by the end of 2025. The panda base also plans to establish more systematic oral health records for giant pandas and further advance research and clinical applications in panda dentistry. "What we aim for is not simply an increase in numbers, but a steady, sustainable, high-quality growth of the panda population," said Wu Honglin, deputy director of the Shenshuping base of the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda. ■ Giant panda Beixia is pictured at the West China Hospital of Stomatology of Sichuan University in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province in January 2026. item.title: China's sea-based rocket launches advance as Haiyang builds full industrial chain
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
HAIYANG, Shandong, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- For Song Wenfeng, deputy chief designer of the structural system for China's Gravity-1 rocket, the most anxious moment came before liftoff, not during it. "The ship was rocking noticeably. We were very nervous during the high-altitude operation," Song said, recalling the work to remove the rocket's protective cover at sea on Sept. 15. He and his colleagues worried about whether the launch could proceed smoothly the next day. At 6 a.m. (Beijing Time), the Gravity-1 Y3 rocket lifted off from a sea launch vessel in the East China Sea, placing nine satellites into orbit and setting a new national record for payload weight and orbital altitude from a sea-based launch. The nine satellites -- eight Qianfan constellation satellites and one ultra-high-speed wireless communications test satellite -- were sent into orbit at about 800 km, with a net payload of more than 3 tonnes. The launch followed a carefully monitored journey that began on Sept. 10, when the rocket left a vertical assembly building at the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport in east China's Shandong Province on a self-propelled modular transporter. The 400-meter trip to the dock took about an hour. "I counted the wheels -- 160 of them," said Zhang Tao, deputy chief designer of Gravity-1. "The main purpose is to keep the transport stable and avoid unnecessary disturbance." Once at sea, the challenges differ sharply from those at a land-based launch site. "The marine environment is complex and changeable. From boarding the ship to launch, we kept monitoring data," Song said, noting that high temperatures, humidity and salt spray can affect satellite and rocket components. There are reasons to persist with sea launches despite the difficulties. Sea launches offer greater flexibility, better mission adaptability and higher safety than land-based launches, said Teng Yao, chief engineer of the Oriental Maritime Spaceport (Shandong) Development Group. They require less prior coordination of airspace and shipping routes, allow launches at various inclinations and ensure rocket debris falls into unpopulated waters, he said. China has completed 28 sea-based rocket launches since its first in June 2019, sending 175 satellites into orbit with a 100 percent success rate. Recent launches from waters off the Yangtze River Delta have helped form an initial "Shandong-Shanghai-Guangdong" sea launch layout. Haiyang now has a complete industrial chain from final assembly to rollout and launch vessel integration, said Teng. The Haiyang Oriental Spaceport hosts the country's largest solid-rocket final assembly and testing facility, with an annual capacity to assemble and test 50 rockets and 50 propellant tanks. It has also attracted 30 aerospace projects, with total investment exceeding 32 billion yuan (about 4.8 billion U.S. dollars). More importantly, the spaceport has moved from service provider to standard setter, said Teng. Three national standards for sea-based rocket launches, led by the spaceport, were recently approved and will take effect in November 2026. They cover general environmental requirements, core metadata requirements for infrastructure, and technical requirements for infrastructure platform selection. The spaceport's industrial capacity underpins the commercial logic behind rockets like Gravity-1. "The core of commercial rocket launches is to send as many satellites into space as possible in the most reliable and economical way," said Xu Guoguang, the rocket's chief designer and commander. Gravity-1's design reflects that commercial logic. The rocket's squat, stubby shape and four strap-on boosters lower its centre of gravity and improve stability at sea while boosting payload capacity, Zhang said. Xu said China has accumulated sufficient technical reserves for reusable rockets, but the main challenges lie in engineering and management rather than research. Reusability must also be pursued with cost efficiency in mind, he added. That cost logic also points to combining sea launch with sea recovery. It would maximize payload capacity without extra fuel for trajectory adjustments, and if launch and recovery areas are adjacent, the logistics and time costs of refurbishment and re-flight could be sharply reduced. ■

item.title: From Tehran to Aichi-Nagoya, 52 years of China's rise through Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
* The 20th Asian Games officially opened on Saturday, offering an opportunity to look back on the transformation of Chinese sport over more than half a century. * China made its Asian Games debut in Tehran in 1974 and hosted the Asian Games for the first time 16 years later. Since then, China has topped the Asian Games gold medal table at 11 consecutive editions and hosted the event three times. * The Asian Games have reflected China's rise in international sport alongside its broader economic and social transformation. NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- The 20th Asian Games officially opened on Saturday night, offering an opportunity to look back on another remarkable journey: the transformation of Chinese sport over more than half a century. China made its Asian Games debut in Tehran in 1974. 16 years later, Beijing welcomed Asia to the Chinese capital as host of the 1990 Asian Games. Since then, China has topped the Asian Games gold medal table at 11 consecutive editions and hosted the event three times. For China, the Asian Games have come to represent far more than competition, reflecting the country's rise in international sport alongside its broader economic and social transformation. MAKING A DEBUT Zhang Dawei still remembers the autumn day in 1974 when, at the age of 28, the basketball player was given the honor of carrying the Chinese flag at the opening ceremony of the Asian Games in Tehran. "I blocked out everything around me," Zhang later recalled. "All I could think about was holding the flag properly and keeping pace with the team." For China, the moment carried significance far beyond sport. The country had been largely absent from international competition for more than a decade. The arrival of the Chinese delegation at Tehran airport attracted considerable attention, with photographs of the team appearing in newspapers in several countries the following day. The athletes soon gave the world another reason to take notice. Su Zhibo won the first gold medal of the Games in the men's free pistol event, while teammate Li Yamin set a world record in the women's 25-meter standard pistol competition. China finished third in the medal table with 33 gold medals. The message was clear: China was returning to the international sporting community. In 1979, China's legitimate seat in the International Olympic Committee was restored, paving the way for Chinese athletes to compete more widely on the world stage. At the 1982 Asian Games in New Delhi, China won 61 gold medals, overtaking Japan, which had dominated the Asian medal table for years. It was the first time China had finished atop the standings, a position it has retained at every edition since. Among the rising stars in New Delhi was 19-year-old gymnast Li Ning, who won four gold medals. He would go on to become one of China's most recognizable athletes and, later, one of its best-known sports entrepreneurs. Looking back, Li said athletes of his generation understood that they carried a responsibility beyond competition. "China had just begun opening its doors," he recalled. "When athletes went abroad, we weren't simply going there to compete. We were also representing the image of our country." A WINDOW ON CHINA In 1983, China submitted its bid to host the 11th Asian Games in Beijing. Hiroshima, Japan, also entered the race, but Beijing ultimately won the bid. Securing the hosting rights was only the beginning. The organizing committee faced a funding gap of around 600 million yuan (89.45 million U.S. dollars). Then, a little girl named Yan Haixia donated 1.6 yuan (about 0.24 U.S. dollars) from her New Year's gift money to the organizers, helping spark a nationwide fundraising campaign. Between 1987 and 1990, people across China donated a total of 270 million yuan to help finance the Games, which is the first major international multi-sport event happened in the country. After retiring from competition, Li Ning turned his attention to business. One of his ambitions was simple: Chinese athletes should be able to stand on international podiums wearing brands produced in their own country. The Li Ning Company sponsored clothing for the Asian Games torch relay and the Chinese delegation's medal ceremonies. The brand's appearance at the Beijing Games proved a landmark moment for China's emerging sportswear industry. On home soil, China's athletes dominated, winning 183 gold medals, nearly twice as many as South Korea and Japan combined. Yet the significance of the Beijing Games went beyond the medal table. At the closing ceremony, the Saudi Arabian delegation unfurled a banner reading "Thank you, China," while Bangladesh's read "Long live friendship." 18 years later, the symbolism of the Beijing Asian Games returned on an even larger stage. On the evening of Aug. 8, 2008, billions of viewers around the world watched as the Beijing Olympic Games opened with a spectacular ceremony. A series of giant footprints made from fireworks appeared to move along Beijing's central axis toward the National Stadium, better known as the "Bird's Nest." That same north-south axis had been transformed by the 1990 Asian Games. Two years later, the Asian Games returned to China, this time in Guangzhou. The context had changed dramatically. China had overtaken Japan to become the world's second-largest economy. Guangzhou's GDP had surpassed 900 billion yuan in 2009, more than half of China's entire national GDP in 1989. The contrast with Beijing 20 years earlier was striking. The 1990 Games had required a nationwide fundraising effort, while Guangzhou was able to rely largely on the resources of a single city and market-based financing to prepare for an even larger event. "Through a city's new path of development, people can see the spirit of reform taking shape across the country and experience the fruits of opening up," said Lin Yanfen, then an official with the Guangzhou Asian Games Organizing Committee. China's athletes once again dominated the medal table, winning 199 gold medals. But public perceptions of sporting success were beginning to change. Sport was increasingly becoming something to participate in and enjoy, rather than simply something to win. With Aug. 8 being designated National Fitness Day and the implementation of national fitness regulations, more Chinese people have been shifting from "watching sport" to "doing sport." 13 years later, Hangzhou took up the baton. China's athletes remained the overwhelming force at the 2023 Asian Games, winning 201 gold medals, an Asian Games record for a single delegation, and topping the gold medal table for the 11th consecutive time. Technology became one of the defining features of the Hangzhou Games, with artificial intelligence, augmented reality and other digital tools integrated into the event. The Games also introduced the first digital torchbearer program. More than 100 million people joined the online torch relay, extending the Games' reach beyond the host city. From China's return to the Asian Games in Tehran in 1974 to the technologically advanced spectacle in Hangzhou, the country's Asian Games journey has traced more than five decades of change. Now, as the 20th Asian Games open, that journey goes on. ■

item.title: China railway passenger trips hit record high in first eight months
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China handled a record 3.32 billion railway passenger trips in the first eight months of 2026, up 3.9 percent year on year, according to the China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway). During the period, the railway network operated an average of 11,508 passenger trains daily, up 5 percent from a year earlier. Responding to passenger growth driven by the country's transit visa-free policy, the railway network recorded over 16.68 million foreign passenger trips in the first eight months, up 33.3 percent year on year. Cross-border rail travel also continued to grow. The China-Laos Railway carried 245,000 cross-border trips, up 39.1 percent, while the Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong high-speed railway handled over 23.4 million cross-border trips, up 10.7 percent, China Railway said. Analysts attributed the record to the expansion of China's high-speed rail network, stronger operational capacity, a rebound in tourism consumption and easier cross-border travel. China has expanded its 240-hour visa-free transit program to 57 countries, with Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam the latest added. The policy has helped fuel a surge in cross-border travel, with Chinese border authorities handling 499 million inbound and outbound trips in the first eight months, up 8.7 percent year on year. China Railway has also worked with local cultural and tourism departments to promote tourism, operating 2,501 tourist trains nationwide during the period. Aboard the Y839 tourist train from Xining to Lhasa, Chris, a 56-year-old British tourist, was traveling to China with his wife and daughter for the first time, with Lhasa as the first stop. Long fascinated by China, he chose the train to take in the plateau scenery. "This train is carrying more than 30 foreign passengers from seven countries, including Thailand, Britain and Japan," said Gai Mingjing, conductor of the Y839 train. China Railway said it will prepare for the upcoming Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday travel rush, improve station and onboard services, and run distinctive tourist trains to give passengers a better travel experience. ■

item.title: China launches new satellites
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
A Long March-2D carrier rocket, carrying a group of satellites, blasts off from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in north China's Shanxi Province, Sept. 19, 2026. Launched at 6:50 p.m. (Beijing Time) aboard a Long March-2D carrier rocket, the satellite group, the PIESAT-2 13-16 satellites, entered the preset orbits successfully. (Photo by Wang Yapeng/Xinhua) TAIYUAN, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China launched a group of satellites on Saturday from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in northern Shanxi Province. Launched at 6:50 p.m. (Beijing Time) aboard a Long March-2D carrier rocket, the satellite group, the PIESAT-2 13-16 satellites, entered the preset orbits successfully. According to the launch center, the launch marks the 668th flight mission of the Long March carrier rocket series. The rocket is a two-stage liquid launch vehicle. Its carrying capacity reaches 1.3 tonnes in a 700-km sun-synchronous orbit. Onboard are four Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites, developed by Beijing-based private satellite maker GalaxySpace. Duan Xiao, chief designer of the SAR satellites, said the satellites are equipped with high-resolution and intelligent payloads that enable real-time processing of remote sensing data in orbit. Such a design will help power the development of smart space infrastructure in the future. ■

item.title: China opposes "secondary sanctions," urges U.S. to maintain stable trade ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China firmly opposes unilateral sanctions that lack authorization from the United Nations and a basis in international law, as well as so-called "secondary sanctions" targeting third countries, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said Saturday. The remarks came in response to a question about the United States signing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law on Sept. 18 (U.S. Eastern Time). The legislation strengthens sanctions against Russia, extends sanctions related to Iran, and authorizes tariffs of up to 100 percent on certain third countries that import Russian oil or natural gas. China has always conducted normal economic and trade cooperation with countries around the world on the basis of equality and mutual benefit, the spokesperson said, adding that such cooperation targets no third party and is not subject to interference or coercion by third parties. China will closely follow subsequent U.S. measures and reserves the right to take all necessary steps to firmly safeguard its national sovereignty and development interests, as well as the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies, the spokesperson said. The spokesperson called on the United States to work with China in the same direction and maintain stable economic and trade relations through dialogue and consultation, while contributing to maintaining the global trade order and the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains. ■

item.title: China eyes strong cultural, tourism industries by 2030
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China will strengthen its cultural industries and tourism over the next five years, aiming to steadily raise their share of GDP, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development, newly released by the ministry, calls for turning the sectors into pillars of economic development and businesses that improve people's livelihoods and sense of happiness. One key target is 8.3 billion domestic trips a year by 2030, nearly 2 billion more than in 2025. Chinese tourists spent 6.3 trillion yuan (about 933 billion U.S. dollars) on domestic trips in 2025. The 2030 target is 7.7 trillion yuan. Market analysis shows tourism spending is increasingly flowing into sectors that blend culture and new experiences into travel. Traveling for concerts, sports events and commercial performances, or to explore places known for revolutionary history or modern industry, is a notable example. "It all points to the same trend: tourists are no longer satisfied with a tour that is just about moving from one place to another, but a trip that can invoke cultural identity, or enable them to express their identity or experience something new," said a report by Meadin Research Institute, a market analytics firm. Such an infusion represents a focus of efforts to boost cultural industry and tourism in the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development. The plan supports industrial tourism based on equipment manufacturing and consumer goods, travel packages featuring farming experiences, and comprehensive consumption scenarios. Other efforts include further integrating sports events with cultural tourism, fostering high-quality ski destinations and promoting deeper links between cultural tourism and transportation. For 2030, the plan pledges to create diverse, immersive and interactive consumption scenarios, while boosting spending on cruise and yacht tours and recreational vehicle camping. To cultivate tour packages and business models that integrate culture and tourism, the plan says revolutionary culture and fine traditional Chinese culture can be used to build an emotional connection and improve the tourist experience. It also encourages employers to ensure paid vacation and stagger holidays to boost tourism spending. GROWING APPEAL FOR INTERNATIONAL TOURISTS Improving tourist experience in China appeals to both domestic and international visitors, especially with continued support expected over the next five years. The World Tourism Cities Federation (WTCF) listed Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Hangzhou and Chengdu among the world's top 20 tourist cities in its latest World Tourism Cities Development Report (2025-2026). China has the most cities on the list, according to the report released at a sideline event during the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services, held in Beijing from Sept. 9 to 13. Joseph Lema, an expert with the WTCF, said competition among tourism cities has moved beyond attractions and visitor numbers. What matters now, he said, is the ability to deliver quality experiences, effective governance and sustainable development. On the way to building strong cultural and tourism industries, China is more confident in realizing its ambitious inbound tourism goal. In the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development, the target is to attract 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030. To reach that goal, China will continue to make travel easier for international tourists in areas such as visa-free policy, payment, tax refund, accommodation and transportation. Easier access and more options, from hairstyling and dental care to traditional Chinese medicine and custom tailoring, will bring longer stays by overseas visitors. "This allows them to see a more authentic, diverse and vibrant side of China," said Hu Yang, senior vice president of Tujia. ■

item.title: World Insights: Greater BRICS expands cooperation, amplifies Global South voice
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Twenty years after its inception, BRICS has grown from an economic grouping into a broader platform for cooperation, with an expanding membership and a widening agenda spanning development, technology and global governance. Following the recently concluded BRICS Summit in New Delhi, scholars said the grouping is opening up more opportunities for Global South countries to cooperate and increase their voice in global affairs. FROM EXPANSION TO DEEPER COOPERATION The BRICS cooperation mechanism was formally launched in 2006, with the first summit held in 2009. The grouping has since expanded its membership and cooperation agenda. Today, BRICS members account for nearly half of the world's population, around 30 percent of global GDP and one-fifth of global trade. "BRICS has not only expanded in membership but also deepened the scope of cooperation," said Mikatekiso Kubayi, senior researcher at the University of Johannesburg, pointing to areas such as energy, culture, transport, technology and security. Marcus Vinicius De Freitas, visiting professor at China Foreign Affairs University and senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, a Moroccan think tank, described BRICS as an invaluable mechanism for managing differences and turning common interests into practical cooperation in an increasingly multipolar world. "China is the driving force behind BRICS, yet its leadership is more consensual, reflecting its win-win perspective in foreign policy and global trade," he said. A STRONGER COLLECTIVE VOICE As BRICS has grown, so too has its potential to give developing countries a stronger voice in shaping global governance. Gan Tian Loo, vice president of the Malaysia-China Public Relations Association, said BRICS countries have built consensus over the past two decades in responding to challenges including financial crises, the pandemic and unilateralism. He said recent proposals place greater emphasis on contributing to discussions on global governance and promoting the equal application of international rules, an issue of particular relevance to the Global South. "Acting collectively in discussions on global governance reform could give Global South countries greater bargaining power than pursuing such calls individually," Gan said. Kubayi said this emphasis on the Global South reflects the original objectives of BRICS, including strengthening the voice of developing countries and promoting access to development instruments for developing and least developed countries. "His continuous reference to the Global South is important because that's the whole purpose of BRICS in the first place," Kubayi said, referring to Chinese President Xi Jinping's remarks on BRICS cooperation. At the summit, Xi called on BRICS to be a pioneer in advancing innovation-driven development, a pioneer in upholding peace and stability, a pioneer in facilitating mutual learning between civilizations, and a pioneer in reforming and improving global governance. Julia Roknifard, senior lecturer at Taylor's University in Malaysia, said such initiatives could help build consensus among Global South countries through practical cooperation. "Through the day-to-day support of each other in tech, health security, agriculture and other areas between BRICS full members, partner countries and the wider Global South, that is how they can strengthen their collective voice and influence," she said. TURNING CONSENSUS INTO ACTION As BRICS enters its third decade, the focus is increasingly shifting toward implementation. Kubayi highlighted the five initiatives proposed by Xi for greater BRICS cooperation: open source and inclusive AI, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry cooperation, intelligent manufacturing cooperation, and science and technology talent development. He pointed to AI as a field in which emerging economies want not merely to adopt new technologies but also to help shape how they are developed and governed. "They should actively participate in shaping international frameworks and standards concerning AI safety, ethics, interoperability and governance," said Luan Camargo, executive director of the Institute for Brazil-China Business Research. Economic cooperation is another area where such efforts are taking shape. In Brazil, Maria Elena Rodriguez, deputy director of the BRICS Policy Center and professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, deems China a crucial partner for Brazil's ecological transition, including through investment in areas such as electric vehicles, photovoltaic equipment and green steel. Camargo said sustainable development and innovation require peace and effective governance, while lasting multilateral partnerships also rely on people-to-people exchanges. For BRICS, the next stage will therefore be measured not only by further expansion, but also by whether existing consensus can be translated into practical cooperation. With China set to assume the BRICS chairmanship in 2027, Kubayi voiced hope that the Chinese chairmanship will give fresh impetus to translating the grouping's expanding agenda into action. "We would expect a BRICS group that is a bit more buoyant about cooperation next year. That is clearly the agenda being placed on the table," he said. ■
